newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian academics, police prepare for showdown.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian academics, police prepare for showdown.

text.p: Striking Nigerian academics from a banned union said on Monday police were preparing to use force to evict them from university campuses when a deadline expires on Tuesday.
The lecturers in Nigeria's 38 universities have been on strike since April, pressing for better working conditions. As a result tens of thousands of students have been left idle.

"We have information that the police will evict the teachers and their families from the campuses from September 10," said a spokesman of the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), who declined to be named.
"The police invasion order is a violation of the tenancy agreement between the individual lecturers and their respective universities."
Nigeria's military government last week gave the lecturers a seven-day ultimatum to resume classes or quit the universities.
Police spokesman Tunji Alapini said police had been given the go-ahead to enforce the government decision.
"We will only do so on request from the vice-chancellors of the universities. My men in all the states are already on stand-by," he said.
A statement from the ministry of education which announced the ultimatum said universities controlled by ASUU risk permanent closure.

Local newspaper reports say that staff at some of the universities are making preparations to return to work. However the strike has so far remained solid in the southwest, heartland of opposition to the government.
The government last month banned ASUU and two smaller academic unions because of the strike.
ASUU president Asisi Asobie said there was a plot to arrest and detain lecturers who refused to return to work.
According to Asobie, his colleagues earn about 3,000 naira ($35.29) monthly, much less than their counterparts in other African countries.
The government of military ruler General Sani Abacha has been under fire at home and abroad for human rights abuses and lack of democracy.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, sank into political crisis in 1993, when a previous military government annulled a presidential election meant to have restored democracy after a decade of army rule.
Students were in the forefront of violent protests against the annulment of the elections in 1993, and against the detention of the presumed winner, Moshood Abiola, in 1994.
